title: He Fell 4 Miles With No Parachute, Through a Glass Roof: The Full Case of Alan Magee
description:
Case 025, the full case file. Alan Magee, from New Jersey, joined the US Army Air Forces after Pearl Harbor and became a ball turret gunner: the man in the steel and glass ball under the belly of a B-17, a space so cramped that there was no room to wear a parachute in it. On 3 January 1943, on his seventh mission, his bomber, the B-17F "Snap! Crackle! Pop!" of the 303rd Bomb Group's 360th Bomb Squadron (named by a pilot who had worked for the cereal company), flew in daylight to the German U-boat base at Saint-Nazaire in occupied France. Flak wrecked his turret and wounded him. He climbed out into the fuselage and found his parachute torn to rags. A second hit took off part of the right wing; the bomber caught fire and went into a spin. Short of oxygen, Magee blacked out and was thrown clear. He fell about four miles (the bomb group's own report says about 20,000 feet, later accounts 22,000) and went through the glass roof of the Saint-Nazaire railway station, which took some of the speed out of him. Accounts differ on whether he was found on the station floor or caught in the steel girders of the roof; they agree that he was alive. He had 28 shrapnel wounds, a broken leg and ankle, a punctured lung and a right arm that was nearly lost. By his own later account, the German military doctor who treated him told him that they were enemies but that he was a doctor first and would do his best to save the arm. He did; Magee recovered fully and never learned the doctor's name. Seven of the ten men on board were killed. The three survivors were held as prisoners of war at Stalag 17B; Magee was freed in May 1945. He received the Purple Heart and the Air Medal, later earned a pilot's licence and worked in aviation. Fifty years after the raid the people of Saint-Nazaire put up a memorial to the crew, and Alan Magee and his wife Helen travelled to France to see it. He died in Texas in December 2003, aged 84. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story, made with respect for the seven men of the crew who died. No one is shown dying and no wound is shown. The aircraft are generic low-poly shapes with no markings, numbers, names or nose art; the men in the station and the camp wear plain coats and caps with no badges or symbols; the medals are plain shapes with no portrait or lettering; the memorial stone carries no text; the map is a chalk sketch, not a chart; nobody's likeness is attempted. Nothing anyone said is quoted: the doctor's words are given only as Magee later reported them, in indirect speech. Staging details such as the airfield, the look of the turret, the fuselage, the harbour, the station, the hospital room, the camp and its gate, the table with the medals, the small aeroplane and the grass airfield, the square, who stood where, and everything Rook does are reconstruction, not record. Narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro).

sound_plan.first_frame: One 'hit' at 0.04 of the first shot as the flak burst outside the turret window (the gate needs an impact in the first second; here it is a story sound), then a crash as the glass cracks.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense for Rook's line, action for the flak, tense for the fall and the re-hook, action for the smash, wonder for the finding, triumph for the doctor, sad for the memorial. No drum loop under the sad segment.
sound_plan.effects: One to three cues a shot, each tied to something visible: hits and crashes for flak, clunks for the hatch and the jolt, whooshes for the fall, ticks for the shard and the glass, heartbeats when he blacks out.
sound_plan.hush: Shot 19 (looking up at the hole in the roof): the music drops out for the breath before 'They find him in the station, alive.'
sound_plan.tragic_beats: Shots 26 and 27 carry one tick each; there is no joke after the landing.
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; measured in the local rehearsal, not listened to.

source_notes: The Short's four pages (Wikipedia, the American Air Museum page for B-17 41-24620, Historic Wings, Vintage Aviation News) were read through a fetch tool on 19 Nov 2026 and cover the raid, the turret, the torn parachute, the blackout, the fall, the glass roof, the 28 wounds, the German doctor, the captivity, the seven dead and the memorial; see the Short's source_notes. For the long version, on 21 Nov 2026, NO PAGE COULD BE OPENED: every host was outside this session's network allowlist, so the added facts were checked only against web-search extracts of the pages listed in sources, and each is used only where the extracts of at least two sites agree. That is why this episode ships as 'ready' (private) and not 'approved'. Added facts and where the extracts support them. From New Jersey, born 1919: Wikipedia (born 13 January 1919, Plainfield, New Jersey) and the American Air Museum person page; the narration says only 'from New Jersey'. Joined up right after Pearl Harbor: two accounts in the extracts (one of them We Are The Mighty). Ball turret too cramped for a parachute: two accounts ('no room for the gunner's parachute'; 'there wasn't room for a normal back-pack parachute inside the turret'); one account instead says the chute he was wearing was ruined, so the narration says only that there was no room to wear one in the ball and that his 'waits up in the fuselage', which is where Wikipedia and Historic Wings have him find it. Seventh mission: Wikipedia and several retellings; the 303rd Bomb Group Association counts it as the group's ninth mission, which is a different count. Aircraft name and its origin: Capt. Jacob Fredericks, who had worked for the Kellogg company, named it (303rd Bomb Group Association and b17flyingfortress.de); the narration says 'named by a pilot who used to work for the cereal company' and names nobody; no nose art is drawn. Turret wrecked by flak and Magee wounded: Wikipedia and We Are The Mighty. Second hit took off part of the right wing, fire, spin: at least two accounts in the extracts; the 303rd's own summary is 'a direct flak hit, went into a spin and blew up'; one retelling blames fighters, which is not used. Blacked out from lack of oxygen and thrown clear: as in the Short. Height: the 303rd's mission narrative says about 20,000 feet (Control Towers; Historic Wings 'more than 20,000 feet'); Wikipedia, the American Air Museum and most retellings say 22,000; Wikipedia also says 'over 4 miles'. The narration gives both figures and 'call it four miles' (20,000 feet is 3.8 miles, 22,000 is 4.2). The speed of the fall is single-sourced and not used. Where he was found: on the station floor (Wikipedia) or caught in the steel girders of the roof (Historic Wings and one more account in the extracts); the narration gives both and decides nothing. Injuries: 28 shrapnel wounds, right leg and ankle broken, lung punctured, right arm nearly severed (two accounts; one adds kidney, nose, eye and teeth, not used); nothing is shown. The doctor: by Magee's own later account, reported on Wikipedia and in two retellings, the German doctor told him they were enemies but that he was a doctor first and would do his best to save the arm; it is narrated only as indirect speech attributed to Magee, never as a quotation, and no line of it is put on screen. Arm saved, full recovery, doctor's name never learned: two accounts. Seven of ten killed, three survivors: as in the Short; the two other survivors are not named and how they left the aircraft is not shown (the extracts do not say). Stalag 17B: two accounts ('Stalag 17B', 'Stalag Luft 17B'); liberated May 1945: Wikipedia and Vintage Aviation News. Purple Heart and Air Medal: Wikipedia and one retelling. Pilot's licence and work in aviation after the war: two sites in the extracts (Wikipedia: a pilot's licence and a range of jobs in the airline industry; We Are The Mighty: a pilot's licence and work in the aviation industry); his retirement and where he lived afterwards are not used (not confirmed twice). Memorial: put up by the people of Saint-Nazaire for the 50th anniversary (Wikipedia, 3 January 1993); Magee and his wife Helen travelled to France for a dedication ceremony, which the 303rd Bomb Group Association dates 23 September 1995 and Vintage Aviation News 23 September 1993 'or 1995'. A B-17 history site and the 303rd's page both have Magee and his wife Helen visiting Saint-Nazaire in late September 1995 for the dedication of a stele and plaque near the bomber's crash site. Because the dates and perhaps the monuments differ, the narration says 'fifty years after the raid' for the memorial, gives no date for the visit, and the labels give none either. The film keeps the Short's staging of a plain stone in a town square, which is reconstruction: the real stele is reported to stand near the crash site. Death: 20 December 2003, San Angelo, Texas, aged 84 (Wikipedia and two more). Kept out because single-sourced, disputed or a quotation: anything Magee or anyone else is quoted as saying, his height, the names of the other crew, the navigator's injuries, the crash site, the size and wording of the memorial, his retirement, the television test of the fall. On-screen labels use only facts from the list above. Staging that is not fact: the airfield and the walk to the bomber, Rook measuring the turret, the pack on its hook, the look of the harbour and the pens, the piece of wing and the spin as drawn, the crawl in the fuselage, the station from outside, Rook on the roof, the hospital room, the plaster cast and the bandaging, the three men at the wire, the gate, the table with the medals (plain shapes, no portrait or lettering), the yellow aeroplane and the grass airfield, who stood where at the memorial, and everything Rook does.
